name: North Face

pitch_detail.notes: 300 feet; vertical step requiring Grade V climbing to first ledge

400 feet; most difficult section with vertical, delicate climbing on unusually hard rock (no specific rock type reliably sourced). Features 120-degree roof sections requiring stirrup aid climbing (C1-C2). Poor natural protection; climbers resort to bolts.
220 feet; Grade V climbing to upper ledge
250 feet; final vertical step to summit ridge

descent_text: Do not plan to reverse the technical wall — virtually every account of climbing Baring's north face describes descending a separate walk-off line rather than rappelling the route from top to bottom. From the top of the wall, traverse west/climber's-left (some parties describe following an old 'base-jumper' boot path) around to a talus field and the notch between Baring's summits, then drop roughly 700 vertical feet through boulders and meadow to pick up a heather trail on skier's left. This connects to a game trail switchbacking down through old-growth forest, a roughly one-mile traverse along the ridgecrest, and then a steep switchbacking trail (~1,500 vertical ft) down to a clearing and old logging road that returns to the Barclay Lake Trailhead — about 3 hours car-to-summit-to-car for the descent leg on the routes this has been documented for. This walk-off is a scramble/hike, not a rappel descent, and no fixed rappel stations are established on it. That said, treat this as route- and finish-dependent: Baring's north face has multiple independent lines topping out at different points, some of which may not connect cleanly to the walk-off gully without downclimbing or short rope work, and the 1961 first-ascent party made long rappels down the upper walls to retreat/descend in fog when the walk-off wasn't known or reachable. If you retreat mid-route, or finish on a line that doesn't top out near the notch, be prepared to rappel — carry a 60m rope and rack for building anchors, since fixed/bolted rappel stations should not be assumed on this poorly-protected, historically loose-rock alpine wall; natural anchors (trees, horns, gear) are the norm. Given this uncertainty, treat rappel count as route-specific and unknown rather than fixed.
approach: Park at the Barclay Lake Trailhead (~2,280 ft, end of gravel Forest Road 6024/Barclay Creek Road off US-2 near the town of Baring); a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the self-issue kiosk. This is the same trailhead used for the Barclay Lake day-hike and for Baring's easier South/West Ridge route, but for the North Face, leave the signed Barclay Lake trail immediately — the climbers' boot path starts behind the outhouse rather than on the main trail. Follow an old, abandoned logging road for about 1/3 mile to a cairn (~2,450 ft) where a rough, unmaintained climbers' path splits off toward the base of the mountain — this is easy to miss and is not marked by any trail sign. From the cairn, the boot path climbs steep, loose dirt slopes and crosses the creek draining the face several times; stay close to the water to keep the correct line, since the tread is faint and frequently lost in the brush. At roughly 4,300 ft — about 2,000 ft of gain and 1.4 miles from the car — the path reaches Couloir Camp, the historic base camp used during the decade-long siege that produced the first ascent; it remains a reasonable first-night bivy for parties who want to break the approach into two shorter days. Above Couloir Camp, the route continues up between two precipitous, brush-and-cliff-covered rock ribs that flank a large couloir (snow often lingers here into August, so early-season parties may want an axe for this section) to reach the base of the North Face's first rock step at roughly 5,500 ft, about 1.8 miles from the trailhead. In total, the lower approach involves fighting through approximately 2,300 vertical feet of dense brush (slide alder, vine maple, devil's club) and forest before any technical rock climbing begins — expect around 7 hours from the trailhead to the base of the wall, and wear sturdy approach shoes or boots rather than carrying rock shoes for this section.
overview: Baring Mountain's North Face is one of the largest and most serious rock walls in the Cascades, rising roughly 3,000 feet above Barclay Lake. It is a committing, infrequently climbed alpine rock and mixed objective with significant loose rock and routefinding.
beta: The route involves four major vertical steps. The lower approach consists of approximately 2,300 feet of brush fighting up steep cliffs through dense vegetation (slide alder, vine maple, devil's club). Establish Dolomite Camp at the base of the first step. The climbing involves vertical, delicate mixed terrain with roof sections requiring stirrup aid climbing on unusually hard rock (no specific rock type has been reliably sourced for this face) with poor natural protection. The crux is on the second step (400 feet) which features 120-degree roof sections and extremely delicate vertical climbing. On the lower brush sections, the first-ascent party fixed hundreds of feet of light ¼-inch rope hung from the brush to assist with load-hauling, with separate lengths of full-diameter climbing rope fixed at the most hazardous spots; double fixed ropes were placed specifically on the first step for hauling loads. Multiple attempts from 1951-1959 failed before the successful first ascent in 1960.
gear: rock shoes (carried for the technical headwall pitches)
single alpine trad rack to 3in with extra small-to-medium cams (0.5-1.5in)
sturdy approach shoes/boots for ~1000ft of brush and heather below the rock
a few slings for anchors — do not trust old fixed pitons in place
fa: Don Gordon (Claunch) and Ed Cooper, July 9-13, 1960
